paragraphs: A big shark is stuck in a canal in South Korea. The shark is over three meters long. It is in the canal for three weeks now. Local people call the shark Bukangi. Many people go to watch it swim.

Rescuers try to help the shark go back to the sea. They use a big net, but the net hit rocks. Experts say that city lights and noise confuse the shark. It cannot find its way out. Rescuers now hope that the ocean water will help the shark swim home naturally.
Scientists say warmer seawater brings more sharks near the country.

paragraphs: In Busan, South Korea, a 3.5-meter shark has been stuck in a narrow port canal for over two weeks after a second rescue attempt failed.

Rescuers tried using a massive 50-meter net to gently herd the animal back out toward the open ocean; however, the operation had to be called off when the net kept snagging on underwater rocks. The shark, believed to be a bronze whaler, has turned into a major local celebrity, and it drew roughly 600,000 visitors to the canal area. Marine experts think noisy surroundings and city lights might be confusing the shark’s senses and make it hard for the animal to navigate out on its own.

Rescuers have now positioned the net to keep the animal close to the sea. They hope changing tides will help it swim home. Meanwhile, researchers note that rising sea temperatures are driving significantly more large sharks toward South Korea’s coastlines.

paragraphs: A large 3.5-meter shark got stuck in a canal in Busan, South Korea, more than two weeks ago. People gave the shark the nickname Bukangi, and around 600,000 visitors came to see it.

Rescue teams tried to guide the shark back to the open ocean twice with the help of water jets and a large 50-meter net. The second rescue attempt failed on Friday because the net got caught on sharp rocks. Experts believe city noise and bright lights are confusing the shark, which finds it difficult to get into the sea. Rescue teams left a net barrier to stop it from swimming deeper into the city. They hope the ocean currents will help it swim out naturally.
Scientists say warmer sea waters are bringing more large sharks near South Korea.
